extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, patent practitioners, inventors, USPTO stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and standards discussed in Senate debate on the America Invents Act (U.S. patent reform), covering procedural reforms, patentability/quality measures, PTO organization/funding, and site-selection metrics for satellite offices. Useful for evaluating proposed patent-law changes and PTO performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 14 exclusion for tax-related software
rubrics_metrics.description: This section does not apply to that part of an invention that is a method, apparatus, computer program product, or system, that is used solely for preparing a tax or information return or other tax filing, including one that records, transmits, transfers, or organizes data related to such filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inserted as amendment language to clarify that certain computer program products/systems solely for tax preparation are excluded from the reach of section 14; intended to exempt routine tax-preparation software functionality from specified statutory changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro entity definition — EPSCoR inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of this section, a micro entity shall include an applicant who certifies that the applicant’s employer is a State public institution of higher education in a jurisdiction eligible under NSF EPSCoR, or that the applicant has assigned (or is under obligation to assign) rights in the application to such a State public institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment expands micro entity status to include public institutions of higher education in EPSCoR jurisdictions and applicants assigning rights to them; intended to reduce fees for inventors affiliated with such institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date for EPSCoR micro-entity provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (d) (EPSCoR micro-entity inclusion) shall take effect 1 year and 1 day after the date of enactment of the Patent Reform Act of 2011.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment No. 152 adds an explicit delayed effective date; Senate discussion notes the change would have no budgetary scoring impact but provides transitional timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization to establish USPTO regional satellite offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorize the Director of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to establish three or more satellite offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: improve USPTO efficiency and quality, increase outreach and connection to patent filers, and enhance recruitment and retention of patent examiners; amendment language aims not to unduly constrain PTO discretion and to permit an open, competitive process for future regional offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO satellite office site-selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria used by the USPTO in reviewing possible satellite locations (applied in 2010): patents granted per capita; scientists and engineers in the State per capita; proximity to law schools and major research institutions; number of patent attorneys and agents; number of teleworking PTO patent examiners; presence of Federal employees; availability of office space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senators identify these objective metrics as reasonable for evaluating potential regional sites; additional qualitative considerations mentioned include central location/accessibility, cost of living, quality of life, and local technology workforce pool to support recruitment and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satellite offices success metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional satellite offices should: draw local scientists, engineers and patent attorneys into the USPTO; increase outreach activities and connection to patent filers; enhance ability to recruit and retain patent examiners; and improve the quality and pendency for patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the intended benefits and therefore evaluation metrics for whether establishing regional offices is successful; Senators contend these outcomes will improve PTO performance and reduce examiner attrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of first-inventor-to-file (first-to-file) priority rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Transition from first-to-invent to a first-inventor-to-file system: priority is given to the first person who filed a disclosure with the PTO explaining the invention and how to make it work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages articulated: easier verification of priority by filing date (reduces discovery into conception dates), public clarity of priority, harmonization with most foreign systems, and reduced litigation costs; protection for small inventors preserved via provisional applications and a retained grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of provisional patent applications to protect small inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional applications provide an inexpensive way for small inventors to protect their patent application while discussing the invention with investors and third parties (noted cost: $110).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional filings secure an early filing date under the first-to-file regime and are recommended as an accessible tool for small inventors to preserve rights during development and negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-issuance third-party submissions of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill allows third parties to submit prior art relevant to a patent application before the patent is issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: enable the public to assist PTO examiners in determining novelty/nonobviousness and help prevent grants of patents on inventions already in the public domain; intended to improve patent quality by leveraging public knowledge prior to grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: New post-grant review available within first nine months
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of a post-grant review of patents that can be sought within the first 9 months after a patent is issued and used to raise any challenge to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: enable early correction of mistakenly issued invalid patents before they cause industry-wide disruption or expensive litigation; aligns with National Academy of Sciences recommendation for improving patent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review reform — adjudicative system and higher institution threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes reexamination is to be run as an adjudicative system, and the threshold for starting inter partes review is elevated to a showing of a 'reasonable likelihood' that a patent is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate debate and PTO input framed the higher threshold as necessary to prevent acceptance of challenges unlikely to succeed, enabling PTO to manage proceedings efficiently and avoid wasting resources on frivolous challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of estoppel from administrative challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill preserves estoppel against relitigating in court those issues that an inter partes challenger reasonably could have raised in his administrative challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection is intended to prevent duplicative litigation and ensure finality of administrative proceedings; it is presented as a protection for patent owners while balancing administrative review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits when litigation is pending and overall proceeding duration limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Impose time limits on starting an inter partes or post-grant review when litigation is pending, and impose a one-year time limit on the duration of these proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural time limits are intended to prevent administrative proceedings from being used for harassment or delay, ensure timely resolution, and provide predictability for parties involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO fee-setting authority and fee retention to address backlog
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorize the PTO to set its fees and ensure that the PTO will have access to those fees (i.e., retain fees collected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senators argue this will enable the PTO to secure necessary resources to work through a large backlog (cited figures: 700,000+ unexamined applications; significant pendency times) and reduce application processing delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness/pendency as a core performance metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of patent-system performance include backlog size and pendency time (time-to-first-action and time-to-grant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate cites backlog and long pendency (average ~3 years; many applications take much longer) as economic harms; reducing pendency is a central goal of reform and is used to justify fee changes and PTO reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent quality standard: novelty and nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality patents are those that are novel and nonobvious; low-quality patents (not inventive) impose monopoly rents and harm the economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms (third-party submissions, post-grant review, improved examination resources) are presented as measures to improve patent quality over the long term by better ensuring novelty and nonobviousness before grant or by early correction after grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes reexamination as administrative, less-expensive alternative to litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes reexamination (and its reformed successor inter partes review) is intended to be a less-expensive alternative to courtroom litigation and to provide access to PTO expertise on technical patentability questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate debate notes that administrative panels of experts are more likely to reach correct technical decisions than juries of laypeople; however, the bill tightens certain procedural aspects, which drew critique from some high-tech stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonization with foreign patent systems to reduce burdens on U.S. filers
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving to a first-inventor-to-file system aligns U.S. practice with most foreign patent-issuing jurisdictions, reducing confusion and inefficiencies for applicants filing internationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alignment is argued to make it cheaper and simpler for U.S. inventors to obtain patents abroad and to clarify what counts as prior art in multinational contexts; debate acknowledges concerns but frames harmonization as net beneficial.
